Yes, many penguin species can survive in warm weather, though the answer depends on the species [d1][d5]. According to the Smithsonian Ocean and PBS Nature, penguins live in temperatures ranging from 90°F (32°C) along Patagonia to -76°F (-60°C) in Antarctica, and some species are "comfortable in temperatures 100 degrees above zero," including Jackass penguins in Namibia/South Africa and Humboldt penguins along the coasts of Peru and Chile [d1][d5]. Approximately 14 species of penguins currently live in warm-climate areas, surviving by stretching their flippers to shade their feet, panting to cool down, and laying eggs in shaded rock crevices [d3]. Humboldt penguins, for example, find warm Hawaiian weather comfortable and can cool off by swimming [d7]. Even cold-adapted species like Emperor penguins have built-in cooling mechanisms — they can ruffle their feathers, hold their flippers away from their bodies, and divert blood flow to release heat — though they are primarily suited to cold environments and can overheat on land [d4][d1]. However, cold-climate penguin species may struggle to adapt if placed in persistently warm environments, as their bodies are optimized for cold [d6][d2].
